questions.question: The four assumptions behind the PPC model are:
options: Two goods only; fixed resources; fixed technology; full and efficient employment
Many goods; growing resources; new technology; some unemployment
One good; no resources; free technology; no workers
Two goods; unlimited resources; perfect knowledge; free trade

questions.question: Every point ON the production possibility curve represents:
options: A combination the economy can never reach
A maximum — the most of one good obtainable given the chosen amount of the other, with everything employed
The single best choice for society

questions.question: Moving from option B (10 wheat, 38 wool) to option C (20 wheat, 34 wool) means:
options: Gaining ten tonnes of wheat at a cost of four bales of wool

questions.question: The diagram "outlaws free lunches by construction" because:
options: Lunches are not one of the two goods
The boundary can never be drawn accurately
Prices are excluded from the model
With everything already employed, more of one good is only possible by giving up some of the other

subtopics.title: Reading the Points — On, Inside, Beyond

questions.question: A point INSIDE the curve is:
options: Attainable but inefficient — resources idle or misused

questions.question: A point BEYOND the curve is best described as:
options: Unattainable today — reachable only if the curve itself moves outward

questions.question: In the schedule, successive batches of 10 tonnes of wheat cost 2, then 4, 7, 11 and 16 bales of wool. This pattern is called:
options: Increasing opportunity cost — each extra batch costs more than the last

questions.question: The PPC bows outward because:
options: Resources are not equally suited to both uses — later transfers come from resources that suit the other good better

questions.question: Which list contains only INTERNAL factors that can shift the PPC?
options: Labour force growth, investment in capital, education and training, new technology
Rainfall, foreign capital, disasters, world demand

questions.question: An outward shift of the whole PPC represents:
A devastating drought would most likely:
options: Move the economy along the curve
Drag the curve inward — an external factor destroying productive capacity

questions.question: Falling unemployment that moves the economy from an inside point toward the curve is:
options: Recovery — using existing capacity, not expanding it

questions.question: The distance from an inside point to the curve measures:
options: Lost output — production that could exist with present resources and does not

questions.question: The chain of consequences from producing inside the curve runs:
options: Lost output raises incomes and taxes
Lost output means lost incomes, then less spending, then less tax revenue — and idle skills and machines decay
Lost output shifts the curve outward over time

questions.question: Long-lasting idleness "drags tomorrow's boundary inward" because:
options: Skills fade, machinery rusts and the discouraged stop searching — the resources themselves deteriorate

questions.question: The two policy tasks, in the order the lesson gives them, are:
options: Shift the curve first, then reach it
First reach the curve by employing what exists; then move the curve through investment, education and technology

questions.question: The "iron rule stitched into the menu" is that:
options: Every dozen jerseys is paid for in shirts — the fixed day makes each combination a trade
Jerseys are always more profitable than shirts
The workshop can sew unlimited garments

questions.question: Drawing the menu as dots and joining them produces:
options: The workshop's production possibility curve — the edge of the possible day

questions.question: A country's PPC relates to the workshop's because:
options: The country's curve is a straight line instead
It is the same idea at national scale — fixed resources, two goods for simplicity, a boundary saying "this much, no more"

questions.question: The FULL day — machines humming, everyone busy — lands:
options: ON the line: a maximum in whatever mix was chosen

questions.question: The LAZY day — a machinist off sick, a jammed machine — lands inside the line, which for a country represents:
options: Unemployment — willing hands with work left undone, capacity unused

questions.question: The DREAM day of 60 shirts AND 48 jerseys is best understood as:
options: Beyond the line — tomorrow's target, reachable only when the workshop itself changes

questions.question: The first dozen jerseys cost 6 shirts but the last dozen costs 18 because:
options: Fabric prices rise during the day
The best jersey-hands switch first; pushing further moves shirt specialists onto slow jersey work — resources are not all-purpose

questions.question: New machines plus an advanced course for a machinist moved the workshop's line outward. The national equivalents are:
options: Investment in capital, education and training, better methods, and favourable external conditions
Choosing a different mix of the two goods
Working the same machines harder for one day

questions.question: A breakdown, an emigrating machinist or a storeroom fire would:
options: Step the line BACKWARD — capacity lost that no clever mix can recover
Move the workshop along the line
Have no effect on the line

questions.question: The three look-alike improvements are told apart as:
options: All three are forms of growth
Mix change and recovery are growth; the line moving is not
A mix change walks ALONG the line; fixing a lazy day walks back TO the line; only the line advancing is growth
They cannot be distinguished on the diagram

questions.question: The lesson's "sharpest point" about South Africa is that:
options: Unemployment is unrelated to the PPC
New machines must always come before jobs
With millions of hands inside the line, the cheapest first growth is walking back to the boundary — employing what already exists
